video_title: Scaling Laws: The Politics and Politicking of AI with Assemblymember Alex Bores
gist: NY Assemblymember Alex Bores, author of the Raise Act, recounts narrowly losing a Congressional primary after a $10M+ super PAC backed by OpenAI, Palantir executives, Perplexity and Andreessen Horowitz targeted him, and argues the AI industry follows a repeatable 'fight it, then call it the ceiling' lobbying pattern that is now recurring in the federal AI-preemption debate.

themes.theme: AI Industry's Political Spending & the Bores Race

insights.claim: Five weeks after Alex Bores declared his Congressional candidacy, 'Leading the Future' - a super PAC backed by OpenAI, Palantir executives, Perplexity, and Andreessen Horowitz - named him the number-one enemy in the country and pledged to spend at least $10 million against his campaign.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, large-scale example of AI-industry money directly targeting a single state/federal legislator over an AI safety bill, a template likely to recur in future AI-policy races.
insights.quote: named me their number one enemy in the country and pledged to spend at least $10 million against my campaign

insights.claim: The Bores primary became the second most expensive primary in American history, with heavy spending both against him from industry-aligned PACs and for him from AI-safety-aligned super PACs partly funded by Anthropic; he lost by about four points.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Signals that AI policy positioning can now mobilize primary-election-scale capital from both industry and safety-focused donors, raising the stakes of future state and federal AI races.

insights.claim: Bores argues the industry PAC's early, aggressive spending against him backfired by framing him as 'the guy standing up to industry,' which rallied other endorsers and support behind him; he expects opposition groups to learn from this and spend later, closer to the election, in future races.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Suggests early anti-candidate PAC spending can be counterproductive, a tactical lesson relevant to predicting how AI-industry PACs will time their spending in future races.

insights.claim: Bores describes campaign money's electoral impact as operating through two channels: direct persuasion of voters via ads and mail, and a signaling effect where visible spending marks a candidate as the frontrunner, influencing which other groups endorse or get involved.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: A general framework for assessing how much a PAC's spending in any race actually shifts outcomes, beyond simple ad-exposure counting.

insights.claim: Bores describes a repeating industry playbook: fight a state AI safety bill 'tooth and nail' while it's pending, then once it passes, declare it 'the ceiling' and lobby against anything further - a pattern he says played out with California's SB53 and is now recurring in the federal AI-preemption framework debate.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: A predictive framework for anticipating industry response to any future federal AI safety standard: expect initial resistance followed by an attempt to freeze further regulation once a bill passes.
insights.quote: That's it. We don't need anything else. Don't do anything.

insights.claim: Leaders of the top three AI labs now say they would support coordinated development pauses if verification/validation mechanisms existed, despite those same labs fighting any pause concept during Raise Act negotiations - evidence the industry's public position on substantive safety measures, not just process, tends to reverse after initial resistance.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Suggests genuine appetite for coordinated pause mechanisms may exist among frontier labs once verification technology matures, an underappreciated opening for future international-coordination policy.

insights.claim: Illinois's newly signed AI safety law borrowed language 'word for word' in places from the original Raise Act's third-party audit section - a provision that had been stripped from New York's final bill after heavy lobbying - showing that provisions killed in one state's legislative process can resurface and pass in another state.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Indicates that lobbying wins against specific AI-regulation provisions in one state are not necessarily durable, since the same language can reappear and pass elsewhere.

themes.theme: Federal Preemption vs State 'Laboratories of Democracy'

insights.claim: Bores argues federal preemption of state AI laws should only follow from the federal government actually 'solving the problem' with a substantive standard, not precede it, and supports states experimenting as 'laboratories of democracy' with successful state policies expected to get raised into national standards over time.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Lays out the core substantive argument shaping the live federal preemption debate (referencing a new 'Obernolte-Trean' discussion draft) that would directly affect which jurisdiction's AI rules apply to labs and enterprise AI deployments.

insights.claim: Bores counters the argument that AI labs cannot operate under 50 different state regimes by noting the same labs already comply with laws in 100+ countries (citing Liechtenstein, New Zealand, and Morocco) without claiming operational impossibility, arguing the 'we can't handle state-by-state rules' objection is selectively invoked only against US states.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Undercuts a core industry argument for federal preemption, relevant to assessing the strength of the compliance-burden case against state-level AI regulation.

insights.claim: Bores concedes some smaller states could see AI labs simply withdraw service if state rules on AI development became sufficiently restrictive, but argues large states (New York, California, Illinois, Florida, Texas, Virginia) carry enough market weight that labs won't exit, preserving genuine room for state-level regulatory experimentation specifically in those markets.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Identifies which specific states retain real regulatory leverage over AI labs (large-market states) versus which are more exposed to a lab-withdrawal threat, relevant for handicapping where the next binding AI regulation is likely to emerge.

insights.claim: The Raise Act as passed required frontier AI labs to publish and adhere to a public safety plan and report 'critical safety incidents' to government; earlier drafts also barred releasing a model that failed the developer's own safety tests and required independent third-party audits, but both of those provisions were stripped after lobbying before the governor signed the final version.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Details exactly which substantive safety mechanisms (own-test release bar, third-party audits) were lobbied out of a marquee state AI law, clarifying the real legal obligations frontier labs face in New York today versus what was originally proposed.

insights.claim: After Governor Hochul signed the Raise Act while publicly criticizing its compliance burden, a subsequent chapter amendment converted it from something closer to a liability regime into more of a transparency regime, which Bores acknowledges as both true characterizations depending on perspective.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Clarifies the actual legal teeth (or lack thereof) of the final New York AI safety law for anyone assessing frontier labs' real compliance/liability exposure in the state.

insights.claim: The final Raise Act reinstated a duty for labs to follow industry best practices, a protection that SB53 (California) had explicitly exempted labs from - a specific difference in legal-liability standard between the two marquee state AI safety laws.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: A concrete point of legal distinction between California's and New York's AI safety regimes relevant to comparative litigation-risk assessment for labs operating in both states.

insights.claim: Research from PNC released around mid-July 2026 found that only about 2.2% of American households have a paid AI subscription, evidence that mainstream consumer AI monetization and engagement remains extremely low relative to the intensity of insider AI-policy discourse.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: A sobering benchmark for AI consumer-monetization bulls: paid-subscription penetration is still in the low single digits nationally, well behind the narrative pace of AI-policy debate.
insights.quote: only 2.2% 2% of American households have a paid subscription to AI

insights.claim: Bores reports the share of voters who dismiss AI as 'a fad or a hoax' is shrinking, but a new skeptical camp is emerging around the idea that AI is real yet the labs are 'in a bubble' heading toward 'another AI winter.'
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Flags an emerging 'AI is real but overvalued/bubble' voter sentiment as a distinct camp from outright AI skepticism, relevant to gauging public tolerance for continued AI capex and valuations.

insights.claim: Bores encountered both single-issue voters who supported him specifically because of his AI stance, and voters who disagreed with him on other issues but voted for him solely because of his AI position - evidence that AI is starting to function as a standalone electoral issue rather than a minor sub-topic of tech policy.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Early evidence that AI policy stances can independently swing votes, a signal for how future candidates and PACs may prioritize AI positioning in campaign strategy.

themes.theme: Path Forward: Audits, Verification & International Coordination

insights.claim: The Trump administration's budget proposal increased funding for the federal AI safety institute referenced in conversation as 'Casey's' (almost certainly CAISI, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation) from $10 million to $27 million even while cutting other programs elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: A concrete, citable data point on federal AI-safety funding direction under the current administration, useful for tracking actual (versus rhetorical) federal commitment to AI safety research.
insights.quote: increased Casey's funding from 10 million to 27 million

insights.claim: Bores argues for continued investment in technology that enables verification of international AI agreements with China and others, on the theory that better verification technology expands the range of credible international commitments and diplomatic options available.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Identifies AI-verification technology as a strategic investment area with direct relevance to future US-China AI diplomacy and arms-control-style agreements.

insights.claim: Bores wants third-party AI audits without pairing them with 'complete absolution from liability' for labs, drawing an analogy to financial (GAAP) and security (SOC 2) audit ecosystems as the model for how AI audits should function.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Provides a specific design principle (audits without liability shields) for evaluating future third-party AI audit proposals and legislation.
